stories.headline: US STRIKES IRAN FOR A SIXTH STRAIGHT NIGHT AS OIL JUMPS 4% AND THE DOLLAR, NOT GOLD, BECOMES THIS WEEK'S SAFE HAVEN
stories.body: US Central Command carried out a sixth consecutive night of airstrikes on Iranian military and logistics targets, sending WTI up 4.00% to $82.11 a barrel and Brent up 2.04% to $85.95, both near one-month highs, as Hormuz shipping traffic thinned and Tehran signaled the Houthis could move to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The S&P 500 fell 1.01% to 7,457.69 while investors rotated into the dollar rather than gold, with the DXY holding near 100.78.
stories.explain: Oil chokepoint risk gets priced into futures the moment a threat becomes credible, since roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits Hormuz and rerouting options shrink further once Bab el-Mandeb is also in play - that's why crude jumped before a single extra barrel actually stopped moving. The dollar, not gold, is absorbing this week's safe-haven flows because the same oil shock that raises war risk also lifts US inflation expectations and trims bets on near-term Fed cuts, which supports a yield-bearing currency more than a zero-yield metal.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS SLIDE TOWARD A BEAR MARKET AS CHINA'S KIMI K3 AND A NETFLIX MISS DEEPEN THE NASDAQ SELLOFF
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.49% to about 28,592.66 as the semiconductor group extended its worst weekly rout since last year's tariff selloff, down roughly 20% from its record on doubts that AI infrastructure spending can keep justifying current valuations. Chinese startup Moonshot's new Kimi K3 model, competitive with leading US models, compounded the unease, while Netflix shares fell more than 10% after revenue of $12.56 billion narrowly missed the $12.6 billion consensus despite an EPS beat.
stories.explain: Chip stocks trade on the market's confidence that hyperscaler capex converts into durable revenue, so evidence that a Chinese competitor can match frontier AI performance for less directly threatens the pricing power baked into demand forecasts for that capex. Netflix's tiny revenue miss drew an outsized 10% punishment because at its valuation the market was pricing near-flawless execution, and a roughly $40 million shortfall against a $12.6 billion consensus was enough to break that assumption.

stories.headline: GOLD HEADS FOR ITS WORST WEEK SINCE JUNE EVEN AS IRAN AIRSTRIKES INTENSIFY
stories.body: Gold slipped to about $3,980 an ounce, down roughly 0.3% on the day and 3.4% for the week - its steepest weekly drop in six weeks - even as US strikes on Iran entered a sixth night. Silver fell alongside it to an eight-month low, with both metals losing out to the dollar as this week's preferred safe-haven trade.
stories.explain: Gold usually rallies on exactly this kind of shock, but it's losing a tug-of-war with two forces working against it: a firmer dollar pulling safe-haven flows its own direction, and oil-driven inflation expectations that make traders less confident the Fed keeps cutting, which raises the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset. When a safe-haven asset falls during a genuine geopolitical escalation, it usually means a competing asset - here, the dollar - is absorbing the flows that would otherwise go to it.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.55% AS TRADERS PRICE JUST A 12% CHANCE OF A JULY HIKE, BUT THE OIL SHOCK CLOUDS THE PATH
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 3 basis points to 4.55% and the 2-year eased to 4.18% after this week's cooler June CPI left futures markets pricing roughly a 12% probability of a Fed hike this month and about 56% by September. That calm is now colliding with a fresh oil shock: WTI's 4% jump on the Iran conflict threatens to reverse the disinflation narrative that pulled yields lower in the first place.
stories.explain: Cooler CPI normally pulls yields down because it raises the odds the Fed can hold or cut instead of hike, and today's move follows that script. But a sustained oil shock works through the same inflation channel in reverse - energy costs feed directly into headline CPI and into transportation costs economy-wide - so if crude's rally holds, the same data that just talked yields lower could reverse course within a month or two, which is exactly the tension the market is now pricing into the curve.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN'S MIKE BOYNTON JR. TAKES OVER PERMANENTLY AS WOLVERINES DEFEND THEIR TITLE WITHOUT DUSTY MAY
stories.body: Michigan promoted interim coach Mike Boynton Jr. to the permanent job after Dusty May left the reigning national champions for the Dallas Mavericks' head-coaching vacancy in late June. Boynton, whose recruiting ties and system familiarity were seen as the best chance to keep the roster intact, now has to defend a title with a staff and roster still absorbing the transition.

stories.headline: GRIZZLIES' CAMERON BOOZER AND WARRIORS' YAXEL LENDEBORG MEET TONIGHT FOR THE SUMMER LEAGUE TITLE
stories.body: No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer and Memphis face No. 11 pick Yaxel Lendeborg and Golden State in Sunday's 9 p.m. ET championship on ESPN after the Warriors eliminated a Lakers team that had won six straight, and the Grizzlies got 28 points from Cedric Coward to beat Houston in their semifinal.

stories.headline: TRAINING CAMPS OPEN LEAGUE-WIDE AS ALVIN KAMARA RE-UPS WITH THE SAINTS AND CONTRACT CLOCKS RUN OUT ON HOLDOUTS
stories.body: Alvin Kamara agreed to a restructured deal to stay in New Orleans as veterans across the league face a July 24 report deadline, with unresolved talks - including the Ravens' Zay Flowers and the Cowboys' George Pickens, who will play 2026 on his franchise tag - now racing the calendar. The NFL's indefinite suspension of Cardinals scouting executive Ryan Gold for leaking draft picks and gambling remains the offseason's biggest disciplinary story.

stories.headline: SEC KICKOFF FAN FEST HITS TAMPA SUNDAY NIGHT AS FOUR-DAY MEDIA DAYS OPENS MONDAY WITH LANE KIFFIN'S LSU DEBUT
stories.body: The SEC's broadcast coverage begins Sunday night with a Fan Fest special ahead of Monday's official start to Media Days in Tampa, where Lane Kiffin makes his first appearance as LSU's coach after leaving Ole Miss mid-Playoff-run. Five first-year head coaches - including Kentucky's Will Stein Monday and Florida's Jon Sumrall Wednesday - headline a conference entering its fourth straight season without a national title.

sports.detail: Four-star cornerback Censere Gaylord committed to Washington on July 11, choosing the Huskies over Georgia and Georgia Tech in one of the cycle's most competitive DB recruitments. He joins three-star in-state corner Maurice Williams as Jedd Fisch's staff builds its next perimeter tandem; no game until the Apple Cup opener vs. Washington State, Sunday, Sept. 6 (1 p.m. PT, NBC).

Danny Sprinkle is rebuilding largely through the transfer portal after Zoom Diallo's departure, anchored by Croatian forward Boris Tisma's commitment. Center Hannes Steinbach went 14th overall to the Charlotte Hornets in the 2026 NBA Draft, the program's highest pick in years.

Rookies reported to training camp Friday; veterans report July 24 with the first of 10 public practices (already sold out) on July 25 in Renton. Seattle will also headline HBO's Hard Knocks this preseason, its first appearance on the show; new OC Brian Fleury takes over after Klint Kubiak left to become the Raiders' head coach.

Detroit closed a 1-4 Las Vegas Summer League with No. 17 pick Ebuka Okorie scoring 27 in the finale. The bigger offseason story is a six-team trade sending Caris LeVert and two second-rounders to Milwaukee for Taurean Prince and Gary Harris, part of a broader shakeup that also included the John Collins signing and Isaiah Stewart's move to Memphis.

Seattle improved to 49-50 (2nd, AL West, holding a wild-card spot) after Julio Rodriguez's walk-off sacrifice fly and a Cole Young three-run homer beat the Giants 4-3 in 10 innings Saturday. The series finale is underway today at T-Mobile Park (1:10 p.m. PT first pitch).

Watch Hormuz chokepoint follow-through - the reinstated 20% cargo toll and roughly 230 stalled tankers in the Gulf keep upside risk in oil prices that could pressure the Fed's rate-cut path

deepDive.title: Chokepoint Economics: How a 20% Toll on the Strait of Hormuz Becomes a Global Inflation Problem
content: Sunday's market snapshot carries over unchanged from Friday because equities are closed, but the story underneath it kept moving all weekend. The US reinstated its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz on July 14, this time charging every vessel a 20% toll on cargo value to transit, and roughly 230 loaded oil tankers are now sitting idle in the Gulf with nowhere to unload. That backlog is the connective tissue between three of this week's stories already in the brief: WTI's 4% jump, gold's underperformance despite the ongoing Iran conflict, and a 10-year yield still trying to decide whether the Fed can keep cutting. Understanding how a chokepoint toll moves through the oil market explains why.

A blockade toll doesn't work like a normal tax, because it isn't optional and the alternative isn't cheaper. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits Hormuz, and the only reroute - around the Cape of Good Hope, or through the also-threatened Bab el-Mandeb - adds weeks of transit time plus its own war-risk insurance surcharge. So a 20% toll doesn't get arbitraged away; it gets passed almost straight into the landed price of crude, the same way a tariff on an input with no substitute shows up nearly dollar-for-dollar in the finished good. That's the mechanical reason WTI jumped 4% in a single session even though not one extra barrel of oil left the ground.

What's easy to miss is what the 230 stranded tankers are doing to the futures curve, not just the spot price. Each one is effectively about 2 million barrels of floating storage that traders can't count as available supply, which is exactly the setup that can flip a market into backwardation - near-term contracts trading above later-dated ones - because buyers are paying up for oil they can actually get their hands on now. The 2019 Strait of Hormuz tanker seizures produced a smaller version of the same pattern: a short, sharp spike in nearby futures and war-risk insurance premiums that outlasted the headlines by weeks, even after that standoff de-escalated.

That's the piece the Fed has to sit with heading into its next meeting. This week's cooler CPI print pulled the 10-year down to 4.55% and left futures pricing just a 12% chance of a July hike, but energy costs flow into headline inflation faster than almost any other input, and a sustained toll-driven price floor under crude works against every disinflation assumption baked into that pricing. The same tension flagged in this week's Fed story - that a 4% oil shock could unwind two months of good CPI data - is exactly the mechanism playing out in the tanker queue outside the Strait right now. The number to watch isn't just next month's CPI print; it's whether that 230-tanker backlog clears or keeps growing before it lands.
